subject: political-science
readings: Ashbee & Hurst (2020), 'The Trump foreign policy record and the concept of transformational change,' Global Affairs 6(1): 5–19 · Putnam (1988), 'Diplomacy and Domestic Politics: The Logic of Two-Level Games,' International Organization 42(3): 427–460 (to p.435)

cards.front: What is the **"black box"** critique that this lecture opens up — and why do the grand IR theories deserve it?
cards.back:
The **"black box"** = grand IR theory treats the state's **internal politics as unopened**: inputs (the international system) → outputs (policy), with nothing examined in between.

The main IR theories work at the **international / state level**, so they **relegate or disregard domestic processes**, treating the state as a unit that simply *responds to the system*. This session **opens the box**: foreign policy is shaped by **domestic as well as international variables**, and the two **interact**.
cards.hint: System in → policy out, nothing examined between.

cards.front: *"International relations are anarchic; trust is limited, so **any** state — democracy or autocracy — must prioritise its own security & survival and act if it has the capacities. Domestic type barely matters."* Which theory, and what does it do to the black box?
cards.back:
**Structural realism (Waltz).**

It keeps the state **firmly black-boxed** — the *type* of regime is nearly irrelevant; what matters is **anarchy**, **relative capabilities**, and the survival imperative. This is exactly the systemic starting point that FPA and neoclassical realism later reach *inside* of.
cards.hint: Anarchy · survival · Waltz.

cards.front: *"Democracies tend to avoid offensive wars — they answer to publics, are tied by trade **interdependence**, and cooperate through **IOs** — but we still don't examine internal processes closely."* Which theory, and who is associated with it?
cards.back:
**Liberal internationalism (Ikenberry).**

It peeks a *little* more inside than realism — it cares about the **character of political *systems*** — but still doesn't open the domestic **processes** in detail. Home of the tongue-in-cheek **"Golden Arches" theory** (no two countries with McDonald's fight).
cards.hint: Interdependence · IOs · Golden Arches.

cards.front: Run the **neoclassical realism** mechanism: how do systemic pressures become *different policies* in different states?
cards.back:
**① Systemic starting point** — realism's basics hold: **relative power** and **anarchy** exert pressure on every state →
**② Domestic filter** — those pressures are **filtered through domestic "intervening variables"**: leaders' **perceptions**, **state–society relations**, **institutions** →
**③ Divergent output** — so **the *same* international pressure produces *different* policies** in different states, depending on the domestic filter.

Slogan: *"structure pushes, but domestic politics filters the push."* This is the theoretical **warrant** for spending the rest of the lecture on domestic variables.
cards.hint: Structure pushes → domestic filter → different outputs.

cards.front: Name the approach: **the study of foreign policy as a product of domestic processes *and* international structure — opening what grand theory left shut.**
cards.back:
**Foreign Policy Analysis (FPA).**

Alongside **neoclassical realism**, it opens the black box: foreign policy = the **interaction of international structure *and* domestic processes** — not one or the other. FPA supplies the *catalogue of domestic variables*; neoclassical realism supplies the *why they filter systemic pressure*.
cards.hint: The whole-lecture project; three letters.

cards.front: Name the **five families of domestic variable** that shape foreign policy — each a lens, none sufficient alone.
cards.back:
**① Individuals / core actors** — leaders' beliefs, style, psychology (the "**great man**" theory).
**② Ideas & ideologies** — the **paradigm** guiding policy (what goals/instruments seem legitimate).
**③ Bureaucratic cultures & sub-cultures** — agencies' operating cultures, **coalitions & factions** inside the executive.
**④ Interest groups & constituencies** — **lobbying, campaign contributions, the revolving door**, geographic constituencies.
**⑤ Public opinion** — mass attitudes constraining leaders (mind **salience**).
cards.hint: People · ideas · bureaucracies · interests · publics.

cards.front: *"The history of the world is but the biography of great men."* Whose line is this, what domestic variable does it name, and what's its blind spot?
cards.back:
**Carlyle (1840)** — the **"great man theory of history."**

It names the **individuals / core actors** variable — leaders' beliefs, style and psychology (e.g. **Trump**: impulse control, short attention span).

**Blind spot:** focusing on individuals **neglects structural forces** — an individual-only focus **underestimates context**.
cards.hint: Carlyle; leaders as history's engine.

cards.front: On the **interest-groups** variable, distinguish **instrumental power** from **structural power**.
cards.back:
**Instrumental power** = **direct lobbying** — groups act on policy through campaigning, contributions and the **"revolving door."**

**Structural power** = business's **leverage from its control over investment and jobs** — power that operates *without* any direct lobbying, because leaders must keep the economy (and employers) onside.

Same actor, two channels: one is what business *does*, the other is what business *is*.
cards.hint: What business does vs what business is.

cards.front: Define **salience** as it applies to public opinion in foreign policy — and give the case that shows its limits.
cards.back:
**Salience** = how much the public actually **attends to** an issue. Except in **acute crisis or heavy losses**, public engagement with foreign policy is usually **LOW** (Durant & Diehl 1989).

**Case:** **Vietnam** disengagement was blamed on the war's growing unpopularity — but salience means opinion bites **mainly under heavy losses**, so public opinion is a real but *conditional* constraint.
cards.hint: How much the public is even paying attention.

cards.front: Trump's **mercurial style** was able to drive US foreign policy directly. Using the **structural counterweight**, explain what *enabled* that — beyond the man himself.
cards.back:
An individual-only story **underestimates context.** Trump's style was *enabled* by the **relative weakness of checks & balances** in the foreign-policy arena — plus deeper trends: **party polarisation**, **party homogenisation**, and a **populist shift.**

Contrast **Truman (1945–53)**, who led the US into engagement via a *mix* of variables: **individual** commitment + shifts in **economic elites** + **strategic** pressure from the USSR — several variables interacting at once.
cards.hint: Weak checks + polarisation + homogenisation + populism.

cards.front: Before judging Trump as a *break*, you need the paradigm he broke from. Compare **Liberal Internationalism (LI)** with the **militant / conservative internationalism (primacism)** it fragmented into.
cards.back:
**Liberal Internationalism (LI)** — post-WWII **open-ended engagement + global leadership**: builds the **UN, IMF, World Bank, GATT, NATO** and a domestic **national-security state** (National Security Act 1947 → DoD, Joint Chiefs, NSC, CIA).

**Militant / conservative internationalism = primacism** (mainly **Republicans**, from the 1970s split): rejects LI's **cooperative** side → **US primacy**, **hard power** used **unilaterally or in coalitions of the willing**, sidelining the UN — **but keeps a moral purpose** (democracy promotion, regime change; Bush's Iraq). Weakened from ~2006.
cards.hint: Cooperative liberal order vs unilateral primacy (still moralistic).

cards.front: Name the concept: **US primacy / preponderance as the organising aim of foreign policy — hard power used unilaterally, sidelining multilateralism.**
cards.back:
**Primacism.**

It is the core of **militant / conservative internationalism** — the mainly-Republican grouping that, after LI fragmented in the 1970s, kept faith in US **preponderance** and unilateral hard power while **rejecting LI's cooperative multilateral side.**
cards.hint: Primacy as the whole point.

cards.front: Ashbee & Hurst distil Trump's first term into a **populist-nationalist paradigm** of **five propositions**. Name all five.
cards.back:
**① The nation is core** — defined by **ethnicity/culture**, not ideals (Bannon: "a nation with a culture — and a reason for being").
**② Zero-sum competition** — nations struggle for **hegemony**; little scope for cooperation (2017 NSS used "competition" **18 times**); the US has been "losing."
**③ Anti-"globalism"** — the nation has suffered from **globalism** and global elites ("the party of Davos").
**④ Trade subordinated to the nation** — hostility to **NAFTA/TPP**; prefer **bilateral** deals where US weight wins; reject multilateral liberalisation.
**⑤ Moral vision abandoned** — no Reagan "shining city" / Bush freedom agenda; **rejects regime change & democracy promotion** ("we are not here to lecture").
cards.hint: Nation · zero-sum · anti-globalism · bilateral trade · no moral vision.

cards.front: In one line: how does Trump's paradigm relate to the **conservative internationalism** that preceded it? (Give the reading's formula.)
cards.back:
**Trump = primacism + economic nationalism + "principled realism"** — i.e. **conservative internationalism *minus the moral purpose.***

He keeps the **unilateral, primacist, hard-power** core but **drops** the faith in democracy promotion and regime change. *In practice:* challenging **China**, **transactionalism**, deals with **Russia/North Korea**, **burden-sharing** demands, doubts about **NATO/collective security**, **protectionism.**
cards.hint: Conservative internationalism minus the moral crusade.

cards.front: Define **transformational change** (Ashbee & Hurst) — the paper's real contribution — and name its **four** linked elements.
cards.back:
**Transformational change** = a **lasting** shift across **four linked elements** — not merely dramatic-but-passing change (drawing on **Polanyi**, historical institutionalism, Skowronek):

**① Paradigm** — the framework of ideas/goals/instruments (**Hall**), until new ideas become **"common sense."**
**② Interests** — new interests grip power; **new coalitions** (Skowronek).
**③ Institutions** — formal & informal institutional **re-ordering.**
**④ Logics** — new **chains of events / incentives** that endure (path dependence).
cards.hint: Paradigm · interests · institutions · logics — and it must *last*.

cards.front: Run the **four-element framework** on the **1940s Liberal-Internationalism** shift. Why is it the reading's *model* of a completed transformation?
cards.back:
**Paradigm:** open-ended engagement & liberal world order becomes common sense.
**Interests:** New-Deal coalition + "Wall Street" Republicans **sideline isolationists.**
**Institutions:** **UN / IMF / NATO** + the domestic **national-security state.**
**Logics:** **enduring** collective-security commitments (they outlasted their authors).

All four shifted **and stuck** → a **completed** transformational change. It's the **yardstick against which Trump is measured.**
cards.hint: The benchmark: all four elements shifted and endured.

cards.front: Now run the **four-element framework** on **Trump (2017+)**. What's the verdict?
cards.back:
**Paradigm:** populist-nationalist ideas — but only **"common sense" to the base.** *(the most dramatic shift)*
**Interests:** FP establishment & peak business **sidelined**; GOP base shifts to **non-college white workers.**
**Institutions:** withdrawals (**Paris, TPP, UNESCO, UN HR Council**), undermining the **WTO**, gutting **State Dept/IC** — *but* **core alliances remain intact.**
**Logics:** weakened trans-Atlanticism; allies edge toward **self-reliance**; TPP revived **without** the US.

**★ Verdict:** the *beginnings* of transformation, but **"incipient, partial and variegated"** — ideational shift strongest; institutional/interest shifts incomplete; logics hardest to read this early.
cards.hint: Incipient, partial and variegated.

cards.front: Define **embeddedness** — and explain why Trump-I ended up only **"proto-transformational."**
cards.back:
**Embeddedness** = ideas become a *lasting* transformation only when **rooted in supportive *interests* and *institutions*** (so they outlive the leader).

Trump's first-term primacism was **pursued inconsistently** and **weakly embedded**: he **marginalised** the national-security bureaucracy but did **not rebuild** it into a self-sustaining machine for the new paradigm → only **"proto-transformational."**
cards.hint: Ideas need roots in interests + institutions to last.

cards.front: Name the concept: **populism is a "crust" laid over other ideologies — a "thin" ideology (Mudde).** Why does the reading lean on it?
cards.back:
**Populism as a "thin" ideology (Mudde).**

It's one of the reading's **two reasons the change may not stick:** (1) because populism is only a **crust** on top of fuller ideologies, the administration could be pulled **back** toward conservative/militant internationalism; (2) the US remains **locked into** its key post-war security institutions. → hence **"proto-transformational."**
cards.hint: A thin crust on top of thicker ideologies.

cards.front: Run **Putnam's two-level game**: how is an international negotiation a *single* game played at *two* levels — and how do the levels connect?
cards.back:
A negotiation is **one game played simultaneously at two interconnected levels:**

**Level I** = **bargaining between the negotiators** at the international table.
**Level II** = **separate domestic discussions** about whether to **ratify** what the negotiator brings home.

The leader sits at **both boards at once**: a deal must be **struck internationally *and* ratifiable domestically.** The connector is the **win-set** — a deal is possible only where the two win-sets **overlap.** This disciplines the claim that domestic & international interact (avoiding analytical **"ad-hocery"**).
cards.hint: One player, two boards, joined by win-sets.

cards.front: Define the **win-set** in Putnam's model — and state the two consequences of win-set *size*.
cards.back:
**Win-set** = *the set of all Level-I deals that would win **ratification** at Level II.*

**① Overlap rule:** a deal is possible only where the two win-sets **overlap** — **bigger** win-sets make agreement **more likely** (but risk a deal your public dislikes).
**② Schelling conjecture:** a **smaller** win-set can give a negotiator **more bargaining power** (see the separate card).
cards.hint: The set of deals your home side would ratify.

cards.front: *"I'd love to accept, but my parliament will never ratify that"* — being **tied down at home is a bargaining asset abroad.* Name this counter-intuitive point.
cards.back:
**The Schelling conjecture.**

A **smaller** win-set (tied hands at home) can mean **more** bargaining power abroad — it **forces the other side to move.** Weakness at home = strength at the table.
cards.hint: Tied hands as a bargaining chip.

cards.front: In Putnam, distinguish **voluntary** from **involuntary defection** — and say what the distinction proves.
cards.back:
**Voluntary defection** — a **rational leader reneges** on the deal by choice.
**Involuntary defection** — the leader **can't deliver** because **ratification fails at home** (Level II blocks it).

**What it proves:** domestic and international politics are **entangled, not separate** — a leader can strike a deal internationally yet still be unable to keep it because of the home board.
cards.hint: Won't deliver vs can't deliver.

cards.front: As an alternative to "it's *always* a two-level game," the deck says the **balance of domestic vs international variables *varies systematically*.** Name the **four** dimensions along which it varies.
cards.back:
**① Time-period** — domestic variables matter **less in acute crisis** (power centralises, the public rallies).
**② State size** — **small states** have **fewer foreign-policy options** (more constrained by the system).
**③ Regime type** — **liberal democracies** are more exposed to domestic pressures than illiberal/authoritarian states.
**④ Policy arena** — some issues draw far **more domestic engagement** — most notably **trade.**
cards.hint: Time/crisis · size · regime · arena (esp. trade).

cards.front: An analyst explains a foreign-policy shift purely by the **relative weakness of domestic checks & balances plus party polarisation and a populist mood** — barely mentioning the international system. Which *variable family* and which *caution* does this trigger?
cards.back:
This leans on the **individuals / core actors** family and its **structural counterweight** — the reminder that an individual-only focus **underestimates context.**

Properly done, it embeds the leader in **structural conditions** (weak checks, **polarisation**, **homogenisation**, **populist shift**) — the neoclassical-realist move of reading the leader as a **filter**, not a free agent.
cards.hint: Great-man story → don't forget the structural counterweight.

cards.front: Why is this lecture the **hinge** of the course — and what's the single red-thread question to ask of any foreign-policy episode?
cards.back:
It's the **hinge between IR theory (lectures I–IV) and real foreign-policy practice:** grand theories set the **international** stage, but **who a state actually is at home** — leaders, ideas, bureaucracies, interests, publics — decides how it plays. The **two-level game** is the *model* of that interaction; **transformational change** is the *yardstick* for whether a shift lasts.

**Red thread:** for any episode ask — *which domestic variables are in play, how do they interact with the international situation, and is the change **transformational** or just a passing shift?*
cards.hint: Theory sets the stage; home decides the play.
